0.title: His Name Shall Be Called
0.essay:
The Bible never gives Jesus just one name. It gives him dozens: Christ and Lord, Prophet, Priest and King, Son of Man, Lamb, Shepherd, Bridegroom, Cornerstone, the Bread of life, Immanuel, Prince of Peace, the Lion of Judah, the Amen. No single word can hold him, so God gives us many, as light needs every colour of the rainbow to show what it is.

A name for every need

Each name answers a need. We are in the dark about God, and he is the Word who speaks. We are guilty, and he is the Priest and the Lamb. We are lost, and he is the Shepherd. We are dying, and he is the Resurrection and the life. To learn his names is to discover, one by one, that there is nothing we need which he is not.

Offices and titles

Three of these names are called Christ’s offices: Prophet, Priest and King. An office is a role someone is appointed to, with work to do. In Israel, prophets, priests and kings were anointed for their work, and “Christ” means “the Anointed One”. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (questions 23 to 26) and the 1689 Baptist Confession (chapter 8), which this commentary follows, teach that Christ carries out all three offices for his people, both in his humbling and in his exaltation. This is called the threefold office. His other names are usually called his titles: not separate jobs, but windows onto the one person from different sides.

Each chapter asks where a name comes from in the Old Testament, what it meant to its first hearers, what it means to have Jesus in that role for you, and what difference it makes on an ordinary day. The study The Person & Work of Christ gives the overview; this study walks slowly round the building and looks through every window. It sits beside The Trinity, God the Father and The Holy Spirit, so that together they show Father, Son and Spirit.

The chapters

Why His Names Matter; Our Prophet: The Word Who Makes God Known; Our Priest: The One Sacrifice and the Living Intercessor; Our King: Son of David and Lord of All; Seated at the Right Hand, Coming as Judge; Son of God and Son of Man; The Lamb of God; The Good Shepherd and the Great Shepherd; Head, Bridegroom and Cornerstone; The Last Adam and the Firstborn from the Dead; “I Am”: Bread, Light, Door, Shepherd, Resurrection, Way, Vine; Immanuel, Wonderful Counsellor, Prince of Peace; and The Lion and the Lamb, the Alpha and the Omega, the Amen.

For reflection

Which names of Jesus do you use most when you pray? Which do you hardly ever use? If you could know Jesus by only one name, which would you choose, and what would you miss?

1.title: Why His Names Matter
1.essay:
Parents today usually choose a name because they like the sound of it, or to honour a grandparent. In the Bible a name often does more. It tells you who someone is, or what God is about to do through them. So when God himself names his Son, we should lean in and listen.

Names that reveal

Abram was renamed Abraham, “father of a multitude”, on the day God promised him a family he could not yet see. And when Moses asked to see God’s glory, God answered by proclaiming his name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). In Scripture, to know someone’s name is to be let into their heart. Each name of Christ is God telling us, in a word or two, who his Son is for us. We begin with the three the New Testament uses most: Jesus, Christ and Lord.

Jesus: the LORD saves

The angel told Joseph, “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua, which means “the LORD saves”. The first Joshua led Israel into the promised land, but could not give them lasting rest (Hebrews 4:8). He brought the people into a land. The second Joshua brings them home to God.

It was a common name, the kind you could shout across a market or a carpenter’s yard. The eternal Son came close enough to be called in for supper. Yet the angel loaded the ordinary name with an extraordinary mission. He did not say “he will teach his people”, or even “free his people from Rome”, which is what many in Israel longed for. He went beneath the politics to the real problem, the one inside us: “from their sins”. Every time we say the name Jesus, we are saying what he came to do.

Christ: the Anointed One

“Christ” is not Jesus’ surname. It is a title, the Greek form of the Hebrew word Messiah, and it means “anointed”. In Israel, oil was poured on a person’s head to set them apart for God’s service: kings like David (1 Samuel 16:13), priests like Aaron (Exodus 29:7), and at least one prophet, Elisha (1 Kings 19:16). By Jesus’ time, faithful Israelites were waiting for the Anointed One, the King God had promised.

Jesus was anointed, not with a horn of oil, but with the Holy Spirit. In the synagogue at Nazareth he read from Isaiah, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18), and then said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). So every time we say “Jesus Christ” we make a small confession: this Jesus is the one Israel was waiting for, the Prophet, Priest and King of the next three chapters.

Lord: the name above every name

The Greek translation of the Old Testament, made before Christ, usually put kyrios, “Lord”, where the Hebrew had God’s own personal name, which English Bibles print as “the LORD”. So when the first Christians called Jesus “Lord”, they meant far more than “sir”. At Pentecost Peter said, “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36).

Then listen to Paul: “Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9–11). Paul is borrowing words the LORD spoke about himself: “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance” (Isaiah 45:23). Paul was a Jew who confessed every day that God is one. He was not adding a second god. He was saying that Jesus shares the one name.

And look at the word “therefore”. As God, the Son was always Lord. But he took our nature and “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), and the name above every name was given to the man who went lower than anyone. The highest name in the universe belongs to the one who took the lowest place. The hands that will receive every bowed knee still bear the marks of nails.

Saying his name today

“Jesus is Lord” was the first Christian creed, and Paul says no one can say it “except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3), because it is not a phrase but a surrender. In the early centuries some Christians were put to death because they would not give Caesar that title. We have other lords on offer: a career, a reputation, our own comfort. Each promises freedom and quietly asks for our whole life. So when we pray “in Jesus’ name”, we are not adding a polite formula. We are coming to God on the strength of who he is: “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

An example

A builder had heard the name Jesus Christ shouted across building sites all his working life, usually when someone dropped a hammer. After he came to faith in his forties, he flinched every time. One lunchtime a younger workmate asked why it bothered him. He thought for a moment and said, “Because it means God saves. And he saved me.” It was the first time he had told anyone at work that he was a Christian.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that the Son of God carried such an ordinary name? Why do you think the angel said “from their sins” and not from their enemies? What other “lords” compete for your loyalty? How might praying “in Jesus’ name” change if you thought about what each of the three names means?

2.title: Our Prophet: The Word Who Makes God Known
2.essay:
We cannot climb up to God and find out what he is like. If we are to know him at all, he must come down and speak. The first thing Christ does for us is exactly that. He is the Prophet who brings God’s word, and more than that, he is God’s Word in person.

Three offices for three needs

Why three offices? The Westminster Shorter Catechism says that Christ, as our Redeemer, carries out the offices of a prophet, a priest and a king. The 1689 Baptist Confession (8.10) explains why we need all three. Because we are ignorant of God, we need a Prophet to show us his will. Because we are estranged from God and even our best service is stained, we need a Priest to reconcile us and present us to him. Because our hearts are turned away and unable to come back, and we have enemies too strong for us, we need a King to win us, rule us and defend us.

John Calvin did much to make this way of speaking central in Reformed teaching. It is not a scheme laid on top of the Bible but the Old Testament’s own pattern: God led his people through prophets, priests and kings, and each of them failed. Jesus is all three, and never fails.

A prophet like Moses

At Sinai the people heard God’s voice out of the fire and begged Moses to stand between them and God. God agreed, and promised more: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18). Prophets came after Moses, but none was his equal, and Israel kept waiting. When Jesus fed the five thousand, the crowd said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!” (John 6:14). After Pentecost, Peter preached that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised (Acts 3:22).

Not only a messenger

Yet Jesus is a prophet unlike any other. The old prophets said, “Thus says the LORD,” carrying a message from someone else. John opens his Gospel with something no prophet ever claimed: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Jewish readers heard in that title the word by which God made the world: “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made” (Psalm 33:6). Greek readers had heard philosophers speak of the logos, the reason running through the universe. John says to both: the Word is not a thing or an idea, but a person. And then the sentence that turned the world upside down: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

So Hebrews can say, “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). The prophets brought pieces. The Son is the whole message. “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). Jesus does not tell us about a God he has heard of, but about the Father at whose side he has always been. He is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), a theme the last chapter of Pictures of God opens up.

The light of the world

At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jewish tradition remembers great lamps lit in the temple courts, said to light up the whole city. Probably in that setting Jesus stood up and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). A prophet sheds light. Jesus is the light. And light does more than inform. It warms, it shows the way home, and it exposes what was hidden. Every true word Jesus speaks does all three.

Having him as your Prophet

What does it mean to have Christ as your Prophet? First, God is not silent. You are not left guessing whether he is angry or kind, whether he forgives. You can look at Jesus and know. Second, he does not only give information. He opens blind eyes. On the road to Emmaus, “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). He still does, revealing God’s will to us, as the Catechism says, “by his word and Spirit”. The Bible does not replace the Prophet. It is the way the Prophet speaks today.

Third, we must listen to all of him. On the mountain of transfiguration the Father said, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Mark 9:7). Timothy Keller often pointed out that if your God never disagrees with you, you have probably made him up. The Jesus of the Gospels comforts and unsettles, often in the same breath. That is one of the marks that he is real.

The Word without a word

The eternal Word, by whom the universe was spoken into being, lay in a manger unable to speak a single word. The preacher Lancelot Andrewes, at Christmas before King James, marvelled at exactly this. The God who once spoke from the fire chose to speak to us as a baby cries, as a carpenter teaches, and from a cross. He came that close so that we could hear him and not be consumed.

An example

A student had built her picture of God from films, friends and her own hopes. A friend invited her to read Mark’s Gospel with him, a chapter a week. She found Jesus saying things she did not like, about money and judgment, and things far beyond her hopes, such as telling a paralysed man, “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Mark 2:5). Halfway through she said, “He doesn’t sound like someone I would have invented.” That was the beginning of listening.

For reflection

What difference does it make that Jesus is not only a messenger about God but God’s Word in person? Where in your life do you most need light at the moment? Which of Jesus’ words do you find hardest to hear, and why? How could you come to the Bible this week expecting the Prophet himself to speak?

3.title: Our Priest: The One Sacrifice and the Living Intercessor
3.essay:
A prophet speaks to us from God. A priest speaks to God for us. We need both, because our problem is not only that we do not know God. It is that we have offended him, and cannot come near him as we are. Christ is the Priest who brings us in.

Names on his heart

In Israel, the high priest wore a breastpiece set with twelve precious stones, each engraved with the name of one of the tribes. God said, “So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place” (Exodus 28:29). Whenever Aaron went in before God, the whole people went in with him, carried over his heart.

Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, he went further, through the curtain into the Most Holy Place, with the blood of a sacrifice. He laid his hands on the head of a goat and confessed “all the iniquities of the people of Israel” over it (Leviticus 16:21), and the goat carried them away into the wilderness. Year after year Israel learned that sin costs a life, and that God in mercy provides a way back. The study Reading the Old Testament Well walks through the priesthood and the Day of Atonement in detail.

A better priest

The first readers of Hebrews were Jewish Christians tempted to slip back into the old system, with its visible temple, robes and smoke. The letter tells them the old ways were shadows, and the reality has come.

The old priests died, one after another. But Jesus “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24). Your priest will never retire, fall ill or be replaced by someone who does not know you.

The old priests were sinners and offered again and again. Jesus “has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27). He is the priest and the sacrifice, and nothing can be added to what he did. That is why the Lord’s Supper is a remembrance and a feast, not a fresh sacrifice.

And the old sacrifices cleaned the outside. “How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14). Christ’s blood reaches the conscience, where guilt actually lives, the voice that whispers at three in the morning.

The one Mediator

“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6). Jesus can bring God and us together because he belongs fully to both sides: truly God, so his sacrifice has infinite worth, and truly man, so he can stand in our place. Because there is one Mediator, we need no other, neither saints nor Mary nor a human priest. Every believer may come straight to the Father through the Son.

The living intercessor

His sacrifice is finished, but his priesthood is not idle. “He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

He is not begging a reluctant Father; the Father who sent him loves to hear him. His very presence in heaven, the Lamb who was slain, is a plea that cannot be refused. And he prays for us personally. On the night before he died, he told Peter, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). Peter still fell, badly. But his faith did not finally fail, because someone was praying for him. In John 17 Jesus prayed for “those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17:20). That includes you. The Scottish minister Robert Murray M’Cheyne said, in effect, that if he could hear Christ praying for him in the next room he would not fear a million enemies, and distance makes no difference.

The Advocate

John adds another title: “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). An advocate is a defence counsel. But see how this one argues. He does not plead that you are innocent, or that your sin was not so bad. He is “Jesus Christ the righteous”, and “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2): the sacrifice that turned God’s just anger away. His defence rests on his own righteousness and his own blood. That is why it never loses.

For us: go straight to him

Because our Priest “has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), he knows the pull of temptation better than we do, for he felt its full weight and never gave way. So comes the invitation: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). The temptation after sin is to stay away until we feel clean enough. That is exactly backwards. The time of need is the time to come.

An example

A young husband fell back into a sin he had fought for years, and for days he stopped praying, telling himself he must first prove he was serious. An older friend read him 1 John 2:1 and asked, “When do you need a lawyer, before you are charged or after?” He prayed that night, and the next week he asked his pastor about seeing a biblical counsellor, so that the fight would not be fought alone. The study Fighting Sin & Temptation says more.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Jesus carries your name on his heart before the Father? Why does it matter that his sacrifice can never be repeated or added to? Do you tend to stay away from God after you sin? How do Hebrews 4:16 and 1 John 2:1 answer that instinct?

4.title: Our King: Son of David and Lord of All
4.essay:
Many people today are wary of kings. But the Bible’s longing for a king is the longing of every human heart: for someone strong enough to put the world right, and good enough to be trusted with that power. Jesus is that King.

A people who wanted a king

Israel asked Samuel for a king “like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). God gave them Saul, and Saul failed. Then he chose David, a shepherd boy, “a man after his own heart”, and David also failed, badly. Yet God made David a promise that outlived all his failures. Through the prophet Nathan he said of David’s son: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Samuel 7:13–14).

Then came the long, sad line of the kings of Israel and Judah, a few good and most not. The last king of Judah was led away to Babylon with his eyes put out, and David’s throne stood empty for nearly six hundred years. But the psalms kept singing about a King to come. In Psalm 2 the nations rage and plot “against the LORD and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:2), and God simply laughs: “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (Psalm 2:6). Isaiah saw “a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1), new life from a dead tree.

David’s son and David’s Lord

The most surprising royal psalm is Psalm 110. “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). David himself calls this coming King “my Lord”. Jesus asked the religious teachers how that could be: “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matthew 22:45). The answer is that the King would be David’s descendant and David’s God at once. Scholars often point out that no Old Testament verse is quoted or echoed in the New Testament more often than this one.

What the first hearers expected

By Jesus’ day, many Jews expected the Messiah to be a warrior king who would drive out the Romans and restore Israel’s glory. Jesus did call himself a king, but he rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, as Zechariah had foretold: “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). He told Pilate, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). He did not mean it has nothing to do with this world, but that it does not come from this world, or advance by its methods.

And then his coronation. Soldiers “twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe” (John 19:2). Pilate fastened a sign to the cross: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (John 19:19). They meant it as mockery. God meant it as truth. This King won his throne by shedding not his enemies’ blood but his own, for his enemies.

The King now

After his resurrection Jesus said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). This commentary holds that he already sits on David’s throne at the Father’s right hand, not waiting for a future millennium to begin his reign; Peter preached Psalm 110 as fulfilled at his ascension (Acts 2:34–36).

He rules his church by his Word and Spirit, as its only Head, a place no pope, government or committee may take. And he rules the whole world by his providence, for his people’s good. God “put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church” (Ephesians 1:22). Every government, every economy, every virus and every election is under the feet of the one who loves the church.

The Westminster Shorter Catechism says Christ carries out the office of a king “in subduing us to himself, in ruling and defending us, and in restraining and conquering all his and our enemies.” Notice the order. He conquers us first. Every Christian is a former rebel whom the King won by love.

His kingdom is here already, wherever people bow to him, and it is not yet complete. “He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). One day the robe will read, for all to see, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16). The study The Kingdom of God traces this story in full.

Having him as your King

To have Christ as King is first to surrender. Psalm 2 ends with an invitation: “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry … Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (Psalm 2:12). The kiss was a sign of homage. But notice that the one we bow to is the one we hide in.

It is also deep relief: your life is not ruled by chance, or by the powerful, or by your own mistakes. And this King says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). Every other lord makes demands and gives no rest. This one gives rest first.

For us: the news and the throne

Psalm 2 does not tell us to ignore the raging nations. It tells us to look up from them. “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4), not because evil is funny, but because it cannot win. We can pray for our leaders, vote, serve and speak up, without despair, because the throne is already occupied.

An example

A retired teacher found herself scrolling the news late every night, growing more anxious and angry. Her pastor suggested that each morning, before opening the news, she read a royal psalm, such as Psalm 2, 72 or 110, and pray for the leaders she was worried about. She still follows the news. But she says she now reads it “from underneath the throne”, and sleeps better.

For reflection

Why do you think Jesus was crowned with thorns before he was crowned with glory? Where do you see his reign now, and where do you long to see it? Which areas of your life have you not yet surrendered to him as King? How might Psalm 2 change the way you read the news?

5.title: Seated at the Right Hand, Coming as Judge
5.essay:
Where is Jesus now, and what is he doing? The Apostles’ Creed answers in a breath: he ascended into heaven, he is seated at the right hand of the Father, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

He sat down

We met Psalm 110 in the chapter on Christ our King: “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). No Old Testament verse is quoted more often in the New, because the apostles watched it come true. On the Mount of Olives “he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9). The Person & Work of Christ tells that story; here we ask what it means for you.

The tabernacle had a lampstand, a table, an altar and an ark, but no chair. The priests never sat down at work, because their work was never done. “And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11–12). He sat because it was finished. Hebrews sums up its argument: “we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven” (Hebrews 8:1). Nothing you do tomorrow can add to his work, and nothing you did yesterday can undo it.

Where two offices meet

Then a surprise: Psalm 110’s fourth verse makes the King a priest: “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). In Israel the two offices were kept apart (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Zechariah foresaw the day they would meet: the Branch “shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne” (Zechariah 6:13). At God’s right hand the Priest of chapter three and the King of chapter four are one person on one throne.

As King he reigns now: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). This commentary reads the present age as the time of that reign: the thousand years of Revelation 20 are now, and the King is “waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet” (Hebrews 10:13). Meanwhile his kingdom spreads through the gospel, one surrendered heart at a time, in every nation.

As Priest he prays: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). The one who rules every event in your life is praying for you through it. His power is never cold, and his sympathy is never helpless.

From there he will come

The two men in white told the staring disciples, “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). This Jesus, the friend they had eaten with that week. And he comes to judge. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and the reason follows: the Father “has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27). God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

Reformed theology places this judgment under his kingly office: the Shorter Catechism’s King is “restraining and conquering all his and our enemies”. What he restrains now, he will conquer then, and every wrong left unrighted will be put right.

“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne” (Matthew 25:31). He separates the nations like sheep from goats. The sheep do not earn the kingdom. It was prepared for them “from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34), and they inherit it. Their kindness to “the least of these my brothers” (Matthew 25:40), most likely Christ’s needy disciples, is the evidence of lives that belong to him. Then come words that cannot be softened: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). The judgment is real and serious for all; Judgment and Hell faces its weight. Believers too “must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10), not to be condemned, but to have their lives brought into the light.

The Judge who was judged

Who sits on that throne? The man who stood bound before Caiaphas and Pilate. They condemned him, and in that condemnation God dealt with our guilt: “he condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3).

The one you will meet that day is not a stranger reading your file. He is the one who took your sentence. The Heidelberg Catechism (question 52) says, in effect, that we may lift up our heads and wait for the Judge, because he first stood trial before God in our place. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and we “may have confidence for the day of judgment” (1 John 4:17). “Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died … who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34).

The day that will make the whole world tremble is, for those in Christ, the day the Bridegroom comes. The face on the throne is the face that wept at a friend’s grave. The hands that open the books still bear the nails. And for anyone still outside, the Judge is today the Saviour who invites, for God “commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).

An example

A man had grown up in a church where Christ’s return was used to frighten children, and for years the word “judgment” tied a knot in his stomach. A friend asked him to read Romans 8:33–34 aloud and to notice where the Judge was sitting and what he was doing. “He is praying for me,” he said slowly. “The one I was afraid of is praying for me.” He still takes the last day seriously. He no longer dreads it.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Christ sat down because his work was finished? How does it help to know that the King who rules your circumstances is also the Priest who prays for you? Why does it matter that the Judge of all was judged in our place? How should the certainty of his return shape the way you treat “the least of these” this week?

6.title: Son of God and Son of Man
6.essay:
You might expect “Son of God” to speak of Jesus’ divinity and “Son of Man” of his humanity. There is truth in that, but both titles have deep Old Testament roots, and Jesus filled each of them with more than anyone expected. Put together, they tell us who he is, and what he has made us.

“Son of God” before Jesus

In the Old Testament “son of God” is used in several ways. Luke traces Jesus’ family line back to “Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38), made directly by God. God told Pharaoh, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). And God promised that David’s royal heir would be his son: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Samuel 7:14). In Psalm 2 the LORD says to his anointed King, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). In Israel’s ears, “Son of God” was above all a royal title.

More than a royal title

But Jesus filled it to overflowing. He called God “my Father” in a way no one else dared. John records why the leaders wanted him dead: “he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). He prayed, “Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). Adam, Israel and David became God’s sons in time. Jesus is the eternal Son, begotten of the Father before all ages, not made, sharing the one divine nature. The study The Trinity explains this, and God the Father explores the Father who has always had his Son.

At his baptism the Father spoke: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11). Before Jesus had preached a sermon or done a miracle, the Father declared his delight in him.

“Son of Man”: the title Jesus chose

Jesus seldom called himself the Son of God in public. The title he used of himself, around eighty times in the Gospels, was “the Son of Man”. Why?

In ordinary Hebrew, “son of man” simply means a human being. God addresses the prophet Ezekiel this way again and again, “Son of man, stand on your feet” (Ezekiel 2:1). But in the book of Daniel the phrase lights up. After a vision of empires as beasts rising from the sea, Daniel sees this: “behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom” (Daniel 7:13–14). After the beasts, a human figure, riding the clouds as only God does, who receives a kingdom that all nations will serve.

So the title was a kind of riddle. It could sound humble, “just a man”, yet it carried the glory of Daniel 7 for anyone with ears to hear, and it did not stir up hopes of revolt the way “Messiah” could.

Three kinds of sayings

Some of his Son of Man sayings speak of authority now: “the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Mark 2:10). Some speak of suffering: he “must suffer many things and be rejected … and be killed, and after three days rise again” (Mark 8:31). And some speak of glory to come. Most astonishing of all, he joins Daniel’s vision to Isaiah’s servant: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The one whom all nations will serve came first to serve them, and to die for them. The heir of the universe had “nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

The two titles at the trial

At his trial before the Sanhedrin, the two titles met. The high priest asked, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” Jesus answered, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:61–62). He was weaving together Daniel 7 and Psalm 110. The high priest tore his clothes and cried blasphemy. He understood exactly what was being claimed.

That is why the idea that Jesus was simply a great moral teacher does not hold. C. S. Lewis argued in Mere Christianity that a mere man who said the things Jesus said would not be a great teacher at all. Either he was badly deluded, or worse, or he is who he said he was. Jesus does not leave us the option of admiring him from a distance.

What this means for you

As the Son of Man he knows our life from the inside: tiredness, hunger, grief and death. As the Son of God he has power to forgive sins and raise the dead. You need both. A God who never became man could not stand in your place. A man who was not God could not save you.

And there is more. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5). The eternal Son of God became a son of man, so that sons and daughters of men could become children of God. And the Father’s delight, spoken at the Jordan before Jesus had done a single miracle, now rests on everyone who is in Christ. It does not rest on your performance either.

An example

A teenager told her youth group that a school friend said Jesus never claimed to be God. The youth leader read the trial scene in Mark 14 with them slowly, and the group noticed the high priest’s torn robe. “If he wasn’t claiming to be God,” one boy asked, “why did they kill him for blasphemy?” She went back to her friend with the passage on her phone, and they talked for an hour.

For reflection

Why do you think Jesus preferred the title “Son of Man”? What does Mark 10:45 tell you about how the King of Daniel 7 uses his power? Which do you find easier to believe, that Jesus is truly God or that he is truly man? What does it mean to you that the Father’s delight in his Son now rests on you in Christ?

7.title: The Lamb of God
7.essay:
Of all Christ’s titles, this is the strangest. Kings are called lions or eagles, never lambs. Yet the last book of the Bible calls Jesus “the Lamb” nearly thirty times, and the song of heaven is sung to a Lamb who was slain. To understand why, we have to go back to a question asked on a mountain.

“Where is the lamb?”

Abraham climbed Mount Moriah with his son Isaac, carrying wood and fire and a knife. Isaac said, “Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” Abraham answered, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:7–8). In the end God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided a ram in Isaac’s place. But Isaac’s question hung in the air of the Old Testament for two thousand years. Where is the lamb? Rams, goats and bulls were offered, but they were only placeholders.

The Passover lamb

Then came the night in Egypt. Each household was to take “a lamb without blemish” (Exodus 12:5), kill it at twilight and paint its blood on the doorposts and lintel. God said, “The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). That night judgment fell on every house in Egypt. In some, the firstborn died. In others, a lamb had died instead.

Think of an Israelite family that night: some calm, some terrified, some strong in faith, some weak. Their safety did not depend on how they felt. It depended on the blood on the door. God did not say, “When I see your faith”, or “When I see your feelings.” He said, “When I see the blood.” The Passover was kept every year after that, and not one bone of the lamb was to be broken (Exodus 12:46).

And every morning and evening a lamb was offered on the altar (Exodus 29:38–39). For centuries Israel woke and slept to the smoke of a lamb.

Led to the slaughter

Isaiah then saw something no sacrifice had shown: a person in the place of the lamb. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). His very soul would be made “an offering for guilt” (Isaiah 53:10).

“Behold, the Lamb of God”

Then, by the Jordan, John the Baptist saw Jesus walking towards him and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). His hearers had Passover lambs, temple lambs and Isaiah’s lamb in their memory. Isaac’s question was answered at last. Here is the lamb. God has provided it himself, and it is his own Son.

Jesus died at Passover time. The soldiers broke the legs of the two men crucified beside him, but not his, and John says, “these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:36). Paul says it simply: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

This is the heart of the gospel. On the cross Christ bore the judgment that our sins deserved, in our place, so that God’s judgment passes over us. It is not that a kind Son persuaded an angry Father. Abraham’s words were right: God provided the lamb. The love that sent him and the justice that fell on him are the love and justice of the one God.

Chosen before the world began

Peter adds something breathtaking: we were ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot. He was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you” (1 Peter 1:19–20). The cross was no rescue plan invented after things went wrong. Before God made the first star, he knew the Lamb would be slain, and he made the world anyway.

The Lamb on the throne

In Revelation 5, John sees a scroll in God’s right hand, sealed with seven seals: the plan of history. No one is worthy to open it, and John weeps, until he is told that the Lion of Judah has conquered. He turns and sees “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). Standing, because he is risen. As though slain, because he still bears his wounds.

Then heaven breaks into song: “Worthy are you … for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Notice what makes him worthy in their song: not first his power, but his wounds. The scars are the reason for the worship. For all eternity the redeemed will look at the centre of heaven and see the price of their welcome.

This Lamb is not soft: Revelation speaks of “the wrath of the Lamb” (Revelation 6:16) against those who refuse him. But for his people the last scene is a wedding: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

For us: look at the blood

Many believers judge their safety by their feelings or by how well their week has gone. The Passover says: look at the blood. Your standing with God rests on Christ’s sacrifice, not on the strength of your faith on a given night. In the Lord’s Supper we do not offer him again. We remember, and we feed on him by faith, and we look forward to the supper of the Lamb.

An example

A man in his seventies could not forgive himself for the way he had treated his first wife decades before. He had confessed it many times, but still felt he had to keep paying. At a communion service his pastor read Exodus 12:13 and said quietly, “God did not say, when I see your regret. He said, when I see the blood.” The old man sat in his car afterwards for a long time. That night, for the first time in years, he did not fall asleep rehearsing the past. The study Regret & the Past says more.

For reflection

How does Isaac’s question in Genesis 22 prepare us for John 1:29? Why does it matter that the safety of the Israelites depended on the blood, not on their feelings? What does it mean to you that the Lamb was “foreknown before the foundation of the world”? Why do you think heaven worships the Lamb for his wounds?

8.title: The Good Shepherd and the Great Shepherd
8.essay:
The New Testament gives Jesus three shepherd titles. He is the good shepherd who lays down his life, the great shepherd brought back from the dead, and the chief Shepherd who will appear. Past, present and future: the whole of his care for his people, held in one picture.

The LORD is my shepherd

Long before Jesus, Israel knew God as a shepherd. David, who had kept sheep himself, wrote some of the best-loved words in the Old Testament: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). Isaiah pictured God coming to his scattered, exiled people with a shepherd’s tenderness: “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). And when Israel’s leaders failed the flock, God promised, “I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11), and also that he would set over them “one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23).

The study The Lord Is My Shepherd explores the real world of shepherds and sheepfolds, Ezekiel 34 and the parable of the lost sheep. Here we look at what it means that these titles belong to Jesus.

The good shepherd: he died

When Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11), his hearers knew their Scriptures. God himself would shepherd them, and so would David’s son. Jesus was saying, quietly and unmistakably, that both promises meet in him.

And then: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The word translated “good” means good in the sense of noble, beautiful, the real thing. Other shepherds risk their lives. This one gives his. Christians have long noticed that Psalm 22 stands just before Psalm 23. Psalm 22 begins, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1), the cry Jesus prayed on the cross, and goes on to describe pierced hands and feet and garments divided by lot. Before the shepherd could lead us beside still waters, he had to walk through the valley of the shadow of death alone, in our place.

He knows his own

“I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father” (John 10:14–15). The measure of how well Jesus knows you is how well the Father and the Son know each other. That is an infinite knowing. He knows the parts of you that no one else sees, and the parts you would rather he did not. And he lays down his life anyway.

A shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). On the first Easter morning, Mary Magdalene stood weeping by the empty tomb and did not recognise the man in front of her. Then he said one word: “Mary.” And she knew him at once (John 20:16). You are not a number in a vast flock to him.

The great shepherd: he lives

Hebrews closes with a prayer to “the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20). A dead shepherd cannot lead anyone. But this one was brought back from the dead, and his blood sealed an eternal covenant. He is not a memory. He leads now, and through him God equips us to do his will (Hebrews 13:21).

If Psalm 22 is the good shepherd dying, Psalm 23 is the great shepherd living: leading, restoring, guarding, setting a table in the presence of enemies, staying with us through every dark valley. His “rod and staff” are his Word and his Spirit, protecting us and drawing us back. When he looked at the crowds, “he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34). His compassion showed itself first in teaching. He still feeds his flock with his Word.

The chief Shepherd: he is coming

Peter, whom Jesus had told three times to feed his sheep, wrote to the elders of the churches: “shepherd the flock of God that is among you … not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Peter 5:2–4). Pastors are under-shepherds. The flock is not theirs; it belongs to the one who bought it “with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). They will give an account to him.

Then, fittingly, comes Psalm 24: “Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory!” (Psalm 24:10). The shepherd who died and now leads will one day appear in glory. The one who carried his flock through the valley will bring them through the gates.

For us: let him lead

To have Jesus as your shepherd means admitting you need to be led, fed and sometimes carried: listening for his voice in Scripture, staying close to the flock in a local church, and trusting him in valleys you would never have chosen. It also means being gentle with yourself in seasons when you can do little. Isaiah says he “will gently lead those that are with young”. The shepherd sets the pace by the weakest sheep, not the strongest.

And if you are a pastor, elder or small group leader, remember whose sheep they are. You are a steward, not an owner. The chief Shepherd sees how you treat his flock.

An example

A mother with three children under five felt that she had failed as a Christian. She used to read her Bible for an hour every morning, and now she could barely manage a verse before someone needed her. An older woman in her church read her Isaiah 40:11 and pointed out the last line. “He knows you are carrying little ones,” she said. “He is leading you gently, at your pace. Take one verse and walk with it.” She wrote John 10:14 on the kitchen wall, and prayed it while she did the washing up.

For reflection

Which of the three shepherd titles, good, great or chief, speaks most to you just now? What does it mean to you that Jesus knows you as the Father knows him? How do you hear the Shepherd’s voice in your ordinary week? Where do you need to let him set the pace?

9.title: Head, Bridegroom and Cornerstone
9.essay:
Some of Christ’s names describe what he is to the whole world. These three describe what he is to his church. He is the Head who gives her life, the Bridegroom who gave himself for her, and the Cornerstone on which she is built. You cannot have him in these roles on your own. They come with his people attached.

The Head: given to the church

The study Pictures of the Church looks at the body, the bride and the temple from the church’s side. Here we look from Christ’s side. Paul prays that the Ephesians would grasp the power that raised Christ and seated him far above every power in heaven and earth. Then he says, “And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:22–23).

Read the middle of that sentence again. God gave him, as head over all things, to the church. The one who rules every power in the universe has been given to a small, often struggling people as their own. The church does not have to fight for Christ’s attention among the great affairs of the world. The great affairs of the world are under his feet, and he is turned towards his body.

In the Bible a head is both the one with authority and the source of life, from whom the whole body “grows with a growth that is from God” (Colossians 2:19). The Colossians were being told they needed something extra: special experiences, secret knowledge, strict rules. Paul pointed them back to Christ. “For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority” (Colossians 2:9–10). You do not need a supplement to Christ. You need to hold fast to the Head.

The Bridegroom: he gave himself

The prophets spoke of the LORD as Israel’s husband, so when Jesus called himself the bridegroom he was stepping into God’s own role. And he added something no prophet had said: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them” (Mark 2:20). Early on, in a conversation about fasting, he let slip a shadow of the cross.

John tells us that Jesus did his first sign at a wedding in Cana. The bridegroom’s family was responsible for the wine, and running out would have been a public shame. Jesus quietly turned six great jars of water into wine, and the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said, “you have kept the good wine until now” (John 2:10). Unnoticed, Jesus had done what the bridegroom was meant to do. The true Bridegroom had come, and the best wine was still to be poured.

Then Paul shows what this Bridegroom is like. “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:25–27). Here the Bridegroom himself pays for his bride with his life, washes her, and makes her beautiful. And now, Paul says, he “nourishes and cherishes” her (Ephesians 5:29), as a man cares for his own body. The church’s beauty is not her achievement. It is his gift.

Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, “and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her” (Genesis 29:20). Christ paid an infinitely higher price for his bride, and Hebrews says he did it “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2). Part of that joy was her.

The Cornerstone: rejected and chosen

A psalm sung by pilgrims going up to the temple says, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvelous in our eyes” (Psalm 118:22–23). Isaiah heard God promise “a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation” (Isaiah 28:16). The cornerstone was the first stone laid, and every other stone was set by its lines.

Jesus quoted the psalm after a parable about tenants who killed the owner’s beloved son (Mark 12:1–11). The builders were Israel’s leaders, and the stone was himself. Peter said it to their faces: “This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone” (Acts 4:11).

Years afterwards he wrote to scattered, despised Christians: “As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:4–5). If you have ever been rejected, notice who the cornerstone is. God builds his house on the one the world threw away, and then builds rejected people onto him. Peter adds, “So the honor is for you who believe” (1 Peter 2:7). The King James Version renders it, “Unto you therefore which believe he is precious.” Both are true.

For us: you cannot have the Head without the body

Many people say they love Jesus but have no time for the church. These names make that impossible. A head without a body, a bridegroom without a bride, a cornerstone without a building: each is a contradiction. Love the church, because he does. Serve it, pray for it, stay in it when it disappoints you, and remember that it is his work that will one day present her “without spot or wrinkle”.

An example

A man in his thirties had watched services online for two years since moving to a new city. It was convenient, and no one asked anything of him. Reading Ephesians 5, he was struck by the words “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” and realised he had been trying to love the Bridegroom while keeping his distance from the bride. The next Sunday he went in person, and stayed for coffee afterwards, which he found harder than the sermon.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Christ, head over all things, has been given “to the church”? Are you ever tempted to look for something extra beyond Christ? What does the wedding at Cana show you about Jesus as Bridegroom? How does it change your view of your own church to remember that Christ cherishes her?

10.title: The Last Adam and the Firstborn from the Dead
10.essay:
The Bible tells the story of the human race through two men. Everyone who has ever lived belongs to one or the other. The first man brought us death. The second brings us life. To call Jesus “the last Adam” and “the firstborn from the dead” is to say that in him humanity has started again.

The first Adam

God “formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). Adam was made in God’s image, to rule the earth as God’s steward and walk with him. Psalm 8 marvels: “what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:4).

Then, in a garden full of gifts, Adam reached for the one thing God had forbidden. And because he stood at the head of the race, his fall was not only his own. “Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). Every funeral, every war and every broken promise traces its line back to that garden.

One man for many

Our culture finds this hard. We see ourselves as individuals, responsible only for ourselves. But the Bible says God deals with humanity through representatives, the way a nation is bound by what its leader signs. Paul says Adam “was a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14).

Here is the good news hidden inside the hard truth. If one man could plunge many into ruin, then one man could also lift many into life. “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). And grace is not merely equal to the damage: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Garden and garden

Put the two men side by side. The first Adam was tested in a garden full of food, and failed. The last Adam was tested in a wilderness after forty days without food, and stood firm on every word from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:1–4). The first Adam in his garden said, in effect, “My will, not yours.” The last Adam, in the garden of Gethsemane, said, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The first Adam took fruit from a tree and brought death. The last Adam “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24) and brought life.

Hebrews quotes Psalm 8 and then admits, honestly, that we do not yet see everything under humanity’s feet. “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9). We do not yet see humanity as it was meant to be. We see Jesus, what a human being looks like when everything goes right.

The firstborn from the dead

“For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). At the feast of Firstfruits the first sheaf of the harvest was brought to God, as a pledge that the whole harvest would follow. Christ’s resurrection is the first sheaf. Ours will follow.

Colossians calls him “the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent” (Colossians 1:18). Firstborn does not mean he was created; the firstborn holds the place of honour and inheritance. But it does mean others are born after him. Paul says God’s purpose is that we should “be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). He is the eldest of a new family.

Paul sharpens the contrast: the first Adam “became a living being”; the last Adam became “a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). The first received life. The last gives it. “Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49).

Not ashamed to call them brothers

Hebrews calls Jesus “the founder of their salvation”, the pioneer who opens the way, “bringing many sons to glory” (Hebrews 2:10). Then it says, “he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

Let that sink in. The risen Son looks at people who fail him daily and calls them brothers and sisters, with no embarrassment at all. A glorified man sits at the Father’s right hand, the first of many.

For us: in Adam or in Christ

The most important thing about you is not your nationality, gifts or failures. It is which man you belong to. In Adam you inherit guilt and death. In Christ you inherit righteousness and life. “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The study Union with Christ unfolds what that means, and What Is Man? looks at what it means to be human.

It also gives hope for the body. Christ rose bodily, and he “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). Your aching joints and failing memory are not the end of your story.

An example

A woman in her fifties lived with a painful illness that would not get better, and some days felt her body had become her enemy. A friend read 1 Corinthians 15 with her and explained the firstfruits. “Jesus’ resurrection body is the first one,” the friend said. “Yours is in the same harvest.” She still has hard days, and she keeps seeing her doctor. But she has begun to speak of her body as something God will one day finish, not something he has given up on.

For reflection

Why do you think God chose to deal with humanity through two representatives? Where do you see the contrast between the first Adam and the last most clearly? What does it mean to you that Jesus is “not ashamed to call them brothers”? How does the picture of the firstfruits change the way you think about your body and its weakness?

11.title: “I Am”: Bread, Light, Door, Shepherd, Resurrection, Way, Vine
11.essay:
In John’s Gospel Jesus says “I am” in two ways. Seven times he says “I am” and then names something we need: bread, light, a door, a shepherd, resurrection, a way, a vine. And several times he simply says “I am”, with nothing after it. To understand either, we have to go back to a burning bush.

The name at the bush

When God sent Moses to Egypt, Moses asked what name he should give the Israelites. “God said to Moses, ‘I AM WHO I AM.’ And he said, ‘Say this to the people of Israel: I AM has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14). God’s name is a statement of pure being. Everything else exists because something made it and keeps it. God simply is: he depends on no one, never began, never changes, never runs out. In Isaiah God speaks the same way, “I am he” (Isaiah 43:10), and most tenderly, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins” (Isaiah 43:25).

“Before Abraham was, I am”

In a fierce argument in the temple, Jesus said, “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day” (John 8:56). His opponents scoffed that he was not yet fifty. Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). Not “I was”, but “I am”. And “they picked up stones to throw at him” (John 8:59). They knew he was taking the name from the bush.

When the terrified disciples saw him walking on the lake in the dark, he said, “It is I; do not be afraid” (John 6:20). In Greek, “It is I” is the same phrase, I am. Job had said that God alone “trampled the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8). And when soldiers came to the garden with torches and weapons, looking for Jesus of Nazareth, he answered, “I am he,” and “they drew back and fell to the ground” (John 18:6). For a moment, the glory showed through. Then he let them take him.

Seven gifts from the great I AM

Most of the seven sayings take a picture the Old Testament used of God or of Israel and say: that is me. And each meets a deep human need.

“I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The day after he fed five thousand, the crowd asked for manna, the bread from heaven their ancestors ate in the wilderness. Jesus said, “the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John 6:33). We are hungry creatures, always looking for something to fill us. He alone does.

“I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). We met this saying with Christ our Prophet. Notice where John places it next: just before Jesus gives sight to a man born blind, saying, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:5). He does not only shine. He gives eyes to see.

“I am the door” (John 10:9). That same healed man was thrown out of the synagogue for speaking up for Jesus (John 9:34). Jesus went and found him, and then spoke of himself as the door of the sheepfold: “If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10:9). A door had been shut in the man’s face. The true door was standing in front of him. Whoever else excludes you, he opens.

“I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). We have already seen that this shepherd lays down his life and knows his own by name.

“I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). He said this to Martha, four days after her brother Lazarus had died. She believed in a resurrection “on the last day” (John 11:24), a doctrine far away. Jesus brought it close: the resurrection is a person, standing in front of her. And before he raised Lazarus, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). The I AM cried at a graveside.

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Thomas had said, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” (John 14:5). Jesus did not give him a map. He gave himself. “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). Many today hear this as narrow. But consider: if there is one God, and we have all wandered from him, a single way home is not narrowness. It is mercy that there is a way at all, and that it is a person who comes to fetch us.

“I am the true vine” (John 15:1). Israel was God’s vine: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Psalm 80:8). But Israel bore bad fruit (Isaiah 5:7). Jesus is the true vine, the faithful Israel. And we are not asked to produce fruit by effort. We are joined to him: “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4). “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5) is a humbling word, and a relief.

For us: who am I?

People today ask “Who am I?” with a new intensity. We are told to find ourselves, define ourselves, create ourselves, and it is exhausting. The great I AM answers differently. You will not find yourself by looking inward, but in relation to him. Hungry? He is bread. In the dark? He is light. Shut out? He is the door. Dying? He is the resurrection. Lost? He is the way. Fruitless? He is the vine. The God who simply is has made himself everything you need, and given himself to you.

An example

In his father’s last week, a man sat by the hospital bed not knowing what to say. His father, a Christian, could barely speak, and the son had long ago drifted from church. So he read John’s Gospel aloud, a chapter each evening. When he reached John 11, his father opened his eyes and whispered the words with him: “I am the resurrection and the life.” After the funeral, the son kept reading. He had gone to comfort his father, he said later, and the words had found him instead.

For reflection

Why did Jesus’ hearers want to stone him for saying “before Abraham was, I am”? Which of the seven “I am” sayings meets the need you feel most at present? How does the story of the man thrown out of the synagogue help you read “I am the door”? How might the “I am” sayings answer the anxious question “Who am I?”

12.title: Immanuel, Wonderful Counsellor, Prince of Peace
12.essay:
These names were first spoken to frightened people: a king shaking with fear, a nation facing invasion, a region sitting in darkness. Into that fear Isaiah announced a child, and gave him names that still steady trembling hearts.

A king who would not ask

Around 735 BC, the kings of Syria and northern Israel marched against Jerusalem. When King Ahaz heard, “the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (Isaiah 7:2). Isaiah urged him to stand firm in faith, and God even offered him a sign, “deep as Sheol or high as heaven” (Isaiah 7:11). Ahaz refused, with pious-sounding words: “I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test” (Isaiah 7:12). In fact he was about to turn to the king of Assyria for help instead.

So God gave a sign anyway, not just for Ahaz but for the whole house of David: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). Immanuel means “God with us”. Many careful readers see a child born in Ahaz’s day as a first, partial sign. But Isaiah speaks of the land as Immanuel’s own (Isaiah 8:8), and two chapters later the child is called “Mighty God”. Only one child has ever filled that name. Matthew tells us who. When Mary, a virgin, conceived by the Holy Spirit, Isaiah’s words came true: “they shall call his name Immanuel (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23).

God with us, to the end

Matthew’s Gospel opens with “God with us” and closes with the risen Jesus saying, “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The study God with His People traces this presence from Eden to the new Jerusalem. Here notice simply this: the first person to hear the name Immanuel was a frightened man who had chosen the wrong saviour. God’s answer to his fear was not a strategy but a presence. When we are afraid, we want a plan. God gives us himself.

Light in Galilee

Isaiah 9 begins in Galilee, the region the Assyrians crushed first. “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). Matthew says this came true when Jesus began his ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:15–16). Why will the darkness lift? “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

A child is born: truly human, with a mother. A son is given: he existed before, and came as a gift. Seven centuries before Bethlehem, Isaiah put the two natures of Christ into one line of poetry.

Wonderful Counsellor

The word “wonderful” in Hebrew is not a mild compliment. It is the word used for God’s miracles, things beyond human power. When Samson’s parents asked the angel of the LORD for his name, he answered, “Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?” (Judges 13:18). This commentary reads the angel of the LORD as the Son appearing before his birth. The one whose name was “wonderful” in Judges is the child whose name is “Wonderful” in Isaiah.

Ahaz had looked for counsel in Assyria. This King needs no advisers: his own counsel is a wonder. In him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). He “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). The wisest thing he ever planned looked like the most foolish: to save the world by dying on a cross.

Mighty God and Everlasting Father

“Mighty God” is exactly the phrase Isaiah uses a chapter later for the LORD himself: “A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God” (Isaiah 10:21). The child is God. “Everlasting Father” does not blur the Son with the person of the Father. It describes what kind of King this is: one who cares for his people as a good father does, and who will never die and hand them on to someone else.

Prince of Peace

The Hebrew word for peace, shalom, means much more than the absence of war. It means wholeness: everything in its place, every relationship right. He brings peace with God: “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Peace between enemies: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Peace within: “my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27). And at last, peace in the whole creation, for “Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:7).

He made this peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). The Prince of Peace was not spared the violence of the world. He absorbed it. The war between God and us ended on his body.

For us: counsel and peace

Facing a decision you cannot see through, you have a Wonderful Counsellor: ask him for wisdom (James 1:5), soak your mind in his Word, and talk with wise Christians. The study Knowing God’s Will says more. When fear shakes you like trees in the wind, you have a Prince of Peace, and Immanuel is with you. If anxiety has become a constant companion, it is right to seek help as well: talk to your pastor about a biblical counsellor, who will also want you to see your doctor. Contentment & Anxiety gives more help.

An example

A mother lay awake night after night, afraid for her adult son, who was caught in addiction. She had tried every plan she could think of. One night she read Isaiah 7 and recognised herself in Ahaz, shaking like a tree and searching for a saviour that could not save. She did not stop loving her son or seeking help for him. But she began, each night, to pray the four names of Isaiah 9:6 over him and over herself, and to fall asleep on the last one.

For reflection

Why do you think God answered Ahaz’s fear with a person rather than a plan? Which of the four names in Isaiah 9:6 do you most need at present? Where in your life do you look for “counsel” in the wrong places? How does knowing that Christ made peace “by the blood of his cross” deepen your understanding of his peace?

13.title: The Lion and the Lamb, the Alpha and the Omega, the Amen
13.essay:
The last book of the Bible gathers up Christ’s names like a choir for the final verse. He is the Lion who is a Lamb, the Alpha and the Omega, the Amen. These are names for the end of the story, and for anyone who wonders how their own story will end.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah

As Jacob lay dying, he blessed his sons, and over Judah he spoke of a lion: “Judah is a lion’s cub … who dares rouse him? The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Genesis 49:9–10). From Judah came David, and from David the long hope of a King.

In Revelation 5, as John weeps because no one is worthy to open the scroll of God’s purposes, an elder tells him, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals” (Revelation 5:5). John turns and sees a slain Lamb. We looked at the Lamb in an earlier chapter; here notice the Lion. John did not hear wrongly. Jesus really is the Lion, with all the strength and royal authority the name promised. But he conquered as a Lamb. The Lion did not stop being a lion when he went to the cross. That was the bravest thing a lion ever did.

And because the Lamb is also the Lion, his gentleness is never weakness. He is safe to come to, but he is not tame. The one who will wipe every tear from his people’s eyes will also put every wrong right.

The Alpha and the Omega

Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. We might say “A to Z”. At the start of Revelation, God speaks: “‘I am the Alpha and the Omega,’ says the Lord God, ‘who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty’” (Revelation 1:8). At the end of the book, the same words come from Jesus: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 22:13). In Isaiah the LORD had said, “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god” (Isaiah 44:6). Jesus takes God’s own title, and the book does not blink.

A to Z means everything in between, too. History is not a random sequence of events. It begins and ends in Christ, by whom and for whom all things were made. Your life, with its unfinished chapters, its mistakes and its unanswered prayers, is held between the Alpha and the Omega. Hebrews calls Jesus “the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2). What he starts, he finishes.

“Fear not, I am the first and the last”

When John first saw the risen Christ on Patmos, with eyes like fire and a face like the sun, he fell at his feet as though dead. Then, he writes, “he laid his right hand on me, saying, ‘Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades’” (Revelation 1:17–18). The right hand that held seven stars was laid gently on a terrified old man. And the reason given for not fearing is the very title that might have made him afraid. The one who holds the beginning and the end holds the keys of death. The door you fear most is locked and unlocked by your friend.

The Amen

“Amen” is a Hebrew word meaning firm, sure, reliable. God’s people said it in response to his word: “all the people answered, ‘Amen, Amen,’ lifting up their hands” (Nehemiah 8:6). It meant: this is true, and we stand on it.

Jesus did something unusual with the word. Instead of saying “amen” after someone else’s words, he said it before his own. When the ESV has him say “Truly, truly, I say to you” (John 3:3), the Greek is literally “Amen, amen”. His words needed no one to confirm them. Isaiah had spoken of “the God of truth” (Isaiah 65:16), and the Hebrew there is literally “the God of Amen”. In Revelation Jesus calls himself “the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14). He is the last word, and the last word is true.

Every promise, yes

Paul puts it unforgettably: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Think back over this study. Every one of his names was a promise, and every one is yes. Will God save me? His name is Jesus, “the LORD saves”: yes. Will God speak, so that I can know him? He is the Word and the Prophet: yes. Can my guilt be dealt with? He is the Priest and the Lamb: yes. Who rules a world that frightens me? He is the King and the Lord of all: yes. Who will judge me at the last? The one who sits at the Father’s right hand, praying for me, and who was judged in my place: yes. Will anyone come after me when I wander? He is the Good Shepherd: yes. Does anyone want me? He is the Bridegroom: yes. Will death have the last word? He is the Last Adam and the Firstborn from the dead, the Resurrection and the life: no, death will not, and yes, I will live. Is God with me, here, tonight? He is Immanuel: yes. And how will it all end? He is the Omega and the Amen. It will end in him, and it will end well.

So the Bible closes with a promise and a reply. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon.” And the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). Our amen is only an echo. He is the Amen. But every time we say it, we are leaning our whole weight on him, and he holds.

An example

An elderly woman in a hospice could no longer read or follow long prayers. Her pastor sat with her and spoke the names of Christ, slowly, with a pause after each. Good Shepherd. Prince of Peace. Resurrection and life. Lamb of God. After each one, in a whisper, she said, “Amen.” He said afterwards it was the truest worship he had ever known.

For reflection

Why does it matter that Jesus is both the Lion and the Lamb? What part of your story feels unfinished, and what does it mean to you that he is the Omega as well as the Alpha? Which of God’s promises do you most need to hear as “Yes” in Christ today? Which of his names in this study will you carry with you, and how will you say “Amen” to it?
